Parasuramesvara Temple

Mukteshvara Temple

Parasuramesvara Temple is about 2.9 m taller than Mukteshvara Temple — about 1.3× as tall.

Parasuramesvara Temple
Date
c. 7th–8th century CE Debated: sources disagree, or this rests on tradition or an estimate. See the note for the competing views. [1,2,3,4]
For curious grown-ups

No building inscription is known, so every date comes from style or letter shapes. Panigrahi (1961) said about 650 CE; Brown (1959) towards the end of the 8th century; R.D. Banerji (reported by Panigrahi) not before the 8th century, from the planet labels on the door. Older writers said about 500 CE (Fergusson, 1876) and the 9th century (Mitra, 1880).

Dynasty
Shailodbhava period Debated: sources disagree, or this rests on tradition or an estimate. See the note for the competing views. [1,4]
For curious grown-ups

Panigrahi (1961) placed it in Shailodbhava times, based on his own date of about 650 CE, but wrote that we do not know whether any Shailodbhava ruler built temples here. Fergusson (1876) thought it 'may belong to the preceding dynasty', before his Kesari kings.

Height
about 13 m (44 ft) Debated: sources disagree, or this rests on tradition or an estimate. See the note for the competing views. [2]
For curious grown-ups

Only one set of figures was found: Percy Brown (1959) gives 44 ft for the tower and 48 ft for the shrine and hall together. This is not an ASI measurement. Fergusson (1876) gives only the plan, about 20 ft square.

Deity
Shiva or Vishnu Debated: sources disagree, or this rests on tradition or an estimate. See the note for the competing views. [1,3,4]
For curious grown-ups

Panigrahi (1961) notes carvings of scenes from Shiva's life. Mitra (1880) reports that the Ekamra Purana names its god Daityesvara. Fergusson (1876) judged it a Vishnu temple from its name and its wall carvings.

Temple type
Not yet verified — see our content policy.

What's special

Look at the doorway of the holy room. A carved stone slab shows the planet gods, each with its name cut into the stone beside it. But one is missing! Ketu, the ninth planet god, is left out. Later temples, such as Mukteshvara, added him. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [1]

For curious grown-ups

Panigrahi (1961) notes that Ketu is absent from the planet slabs of all the early temples up to the end of the 9th century.

Step up to the porch hall. It has lasted well, so it shows us what early porch halls looked like. Its middle roof is raised higher than the rest. Stone windows, carved with holes, let the daylight in. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [1,2,3]

For curious grown-ups

The sources give different numbers of doors for the hall (Panigrahi two, Brown three), so no count is given here.

Of all the early temples still in fair shape, this one has the most carvings. High on the porch hall, rows of horses and elephants march along in a parade. Lower down, other panels tell stories of the gods. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [1,3]

For curious grown-ups

Mitra (1880) reads the lower porch panels as scenes from Rama's life; Panigrahi (1961) speaks of scenes from Shiva's life. They may be describing different panels.

Mukteshvara Temple
Date
c. 966–975 CE Debated: sources disagree, or this rests on tradition or an estimate. See the note for the competing views. [1,2]
For curious grown-ups

Percy Brown (1959) judged from details of its style that it was 'probably built about' 975 CE. K.C. Panigrahi (1961) argued for 966 CE. He took that year from a palm-leaf manuscript verse about a Shiva temple, and linked it to this temple through a local tradition that a king called Yayati Kesari built it. Panigrahi also places it between the Sisiresvara (c. 800 CE) and the Brahmesvara (c. 1060 CE). No inscription dates the temple. The research report's 'Brown c. 950' is not supported by Brown's text.

Dynasty
Somavamshi (Kesari) Debated: sources disagree, or this rests on tradition or an estimate. See the note for the competing views. [1]
For curious grown-ups

This is one scholar's view. Panigrahi bases it on the temple's style and on a local tradition that a king called Yayati Kesari built it, whom he identifies as the Somavamshi ruler Yayati I. Percy Brown (1959) dates the temple but names no dynasty in the passage checked. No inscription links the temple to a dynasty.

Height
about 10.5 m (35 ft) Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [1,2]
For curious grown-ups

Brown: the tower is 'hardly 35 feet high'. Panigrahi: 'a height of only 34' feet, with an unclear fraction in the scan text. Rajendralala Mitra (1880) gives 'barely 3S feet' (scan text unclear: 35 or 38). None of these is an ASI measurement.

Deity
Not yet verified — see our content policy.
Temple type
pancharatha shrine with pidha jagamohana Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [1]

What's special

In front stands a free-standing gateway called a torana (arched gateway). Two carved pillars hold up a round arch. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [1,2,3]

Percy Brown called the arch one of the most original ideas in the whole Odisha style. In 1961, K.C. Panigrahi noted that no other surviving temple in Bhubaneswar has such an arch. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [1,2]

Scholars have praised its beauty. Percy Brown called it 'a miniature gem of architecture'. James Fergusson wrote that, in its class, it was 'the gem of Orissan architecture'. Scholarly view: the consensus of scholars from stylistic or indirect evidence, or a single accepted source. [2,4]
